message.reasoning:
We need to produce a test class that covers the JSON test cases, using JUnit5 and Mockito. The provided test class already has some tests, but we need to generate new tests covering all cases: buy and sell calculations, zero division, NaN, null handling, etc. Use parameterized tests where appropriate.

We must not modify @Before/@After methods. Use the existing setup fields? The test class already defines longPosition and shortPosition based on Trade.buyAt etc. However we need to test getGrossReturn with arbitrary entryPrice and exitPrice values independent of the Position's entry type? The method uses getEntry().isBuy() to decide branch. So we need to create Position objects with entry trade type (BUY or SELL) accordingly. For each test case, we need a Position with appropriate entry type. We can reuse longPosition for BUY and shortPosition for SELL. However for cases where entryPrice is zero etc., we need to test the method directly with those entry/exit values, but the Position's entry type remains same. That's fine.

Edge cases: entryPrice null => NullPointerException. Since the method will call entryPrice.dividedBy(entryPrice) etc., passing null will cause NPE. We'll test that.

Similarly exitPrice null.

Division by zero: depending on Num implementation (DecimalNum). In ta4j, DecimalNum division by zero throws ArithmeticException. We'll assertThrows.

NaN handling: DecimalNum has NaN constant? In code they import static org.ta4j.core.num.NaN.NaN; So NaN is a Num. We can use DecimalNum.valueOf("NaN")? Not sure. The library has DecimalNum class with static method NaN? Actually there is class DecimalNum extends Num, with static method NaN? We'll assume DecimalNum.NaN() or DecimalNum.valueOf("NaN") maybe. Safer: use DecimalNum.NaN. But we need import. We'll use DecimalNum.NaN.

We also need tests for zero price exit for BUY (expected 0) and SELL (expected 2). In JSON, they have group "Zero price edge cases". For SELL, expected 2.

Also test calculations for buy and sell positions with given numbers, using DecimalNum.

We'll write parameterized test for each group.

We'll need to create Position objects for BUY and SELL: use longPosition and shortPosition from setup. However those positions have specific entry price (10,20). But the method uses entryPrice param passed, not the internal entry price. So the entry trade type determines branch only. So we can use the same Position objects but pass arbitrary entryPrice/exitPrice values.

Thus in parameterized test, we need to pass a Position (or boolean isBuy) to decide which branch. We'll use @MethodSource to supply arguments: Position, entryPrice, exitPrice, expected, description.

For expected being exception, we need separate test method expecting exception.

We'll create two parameterized tests: one for successful returns (expected Num), one for exception cases.

For NaN and null, also test.

We'll need imports: org.junit.jupiter.params.ParameterizedTest, org.junit.jupiter.params.provider.MethodSource, org.junit.jupiter.params.provider.Arguments, java.util.stream.Stream, static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.*.

We'll also need MockitoExtension import, but not needed for mocking.

We'll keep the existing tests as they are; we can add new tests after them.

Make sure to use DecimalNum for consistency.

Implementation details:

Method source for successful returns:

static Stream<Arguments> provideBuyGrossReturnCases() { return Stream.of( Arguments.of(longPosition, DecimalNum.valueOf("100"), DecimalNum.valueOf("150"), DecimalNum.valueOf("1.5")), ... ) }

But we need to import DecimalNum.

Similarly for sell cases.

For zero price exit: entryPrice 100, exitPrice 0.

For sell zero exit: expected 2.

For buy zero zero division: expect ArithmeticException.

For sell zero zero division: same.

For null entry: pass null.

But method signature expects Num, so passing null compile fine.

We'll have separate test expecting exception.

For NaN: use DecimalNum.NaN.

Implementation of expected NaN: assertTrue(actual.isNaN()) maybe. There's method isNaN? Not sure. In Num interface there is isNaN? Might be. We'll just assertEquals(DecimalNum.NaN, actual). Use assertEquals.

Now produce final code.
